title: Funny Cybersecurity Jokes and Memes Your Team Will Get
summary: Original cybersecurity jokes, the meme themes security teams share, and how to use humor at work without undermining real security advice.
body_markdown:
Cybersecurity humor works because it is built on pain every security professional knows: weak passwords, ignored training, Friday-afternoon audits and the update prompt that never gets clicked. Below you will find original jokes you can use today, the meme themes that keep coming back and why they resonate. You will also find a practical way to use humor at work without it replacing real security guidance.

## TL;DR


- Security humor lands when it names a shared frustration: passwords, phishing clicks, compliance paperwork, on-call shifts and understaffed teams.
- Memes are a form of communal coping, and they also carry real points about basic controls such as patching and multifactor authentication.
- Used with care, humor can make security training more memorable. It should support a communication goal and never replace a procedure.
- Keep it inclusive, never aim it at individuals or sensitive company events, and pilot it before a wider rollout.
- The funniest topic of all, the endless security questionnaire, is also one you can fix with better process and tooling.

## Why cybersecurity is such fertile ground for jokes


Security work is a strange mix of high stakes and repetitive routine. You protect critical systems, yet a good share of your week goes to reminding people to update software, explaining why a password manager beats a sticky note, and justifying budget. That gap between the seriousness of the job and the ordinariness of the problems is where comedy lives.


ISACA's analysis of popular security memes makes the point well. In its[2022 review of five cybersecurity memes](https://www.isaca.org/resources/news-and-trends/isaca-now-blog/2022/five-cybersecurity-memes-and-what-they-say-about-cybersecurity-today) , it argues that memes resonate because they reflect painful industry realities: security tools nobody uses, blame landing on the security team after a breach, outsiders who do not care about infosec concerns, a fascination with shiny technology over fundamentals, and teams that are too small for the job.


A second reason is that the vocabulary is already funny. Firewall, phishing, cookies, bugs, worms, zero trust and attachments all double as ordinary words, which makes puns nearly automatic. That is why jokes built on these terms show up in team chats, training slides and newsletters alike.


A third reason is social.[Atera's roundup of IT security memes](https://www.atera.com/blog/the-best-it-security-memes/) shows that much of this humor is communal coping. Professionals laugh together about recurring friction with users, executives, compliance processes, awareness training and authentication requirements. Sharing a meme says, "You are not the only one who has had this conversation five times this month."


## Cybersecurity jokes to steal


These are original lines written for this article, so you can use them in a team chat, a slide or a newsletter. We grouped them by the situation they poke fun at.


### Passwords and authentication


- Our password policy requires eight characters, one number and one symbol. Users responded with "Password1!" and a sense of accomplishment.
- The best password is the one nobody can guess, including you, which is why we use a password manager.
- Multifactor authentication is like a seatbelt: everyone agrees it is a great idea until they have to buckle it.
- I told my team to rotate passwords more often. Now there is a sticky note on the monitor that says "Spring2" and another that says "Summer2".


### Phishing and awareness training


- Phishing training has a 100 percent success rate: everyone agrees the email looked suspicious right after they clicked it.
- The attacker said the invoice was urgent. The finance team said that was their normal Tuesday.
- Why did the phishing email feel so personal? It had my name, my manager's name and a hopeful attachment.
- Our awareness training is mandatory, which is why the completion rate is high and the retention rate is a mystery.


### Patching and updates


- There are two kinds of systems: those that are patched, and those with a great story about why they are not.
- "Remind me tomorrow" is the most dangerous button in computing.
- Legacy servers are like houseplants in an office. Nobody remembers who owns them, and everyone is afraid to touch them.


### Zero trust, firewalls and cloud


- Zero trust is a great relationship philosophy for a firewall and a terrible one for a family dinner.
- I trust my firewall. That is the problem, and also why it has a very long rule list.
- Why did the IT team skip setting up a remote office on the beach? Too many clouds, too little signal.
- A flat network is just a very honest office with no doors.


### On-call and incident response


- Nothing builds team spirit like three people staring at one log file at 2 a.m., each convinced it is somebody else's service.
- Incident response plan: step one, panic quietly. Step two, open the runbook. Step three, find out the runbook was last updated before the cloud migration.
- The rotation ends, the pager goes silent, and somehow the phone still buzzes in your pocket.


## The meme themes that never go away


If you scan the collections on the first page of search results, the same themes repeat. That is useful: it tells you which jokes are safe and relatable for a broad security audience. The table below summarizes the recurring subjects and where they come from.

Two of these deserve a closer look because they carry real guidance underneath the laugh.


### Basic controls versus expensive tools


ISACA frames patching, strong passwords, multifactor authentication and user awareness as a recurring comic contrast with expensive or fashionable security products. The joke is that a company can spend heavily on an advanced platform while an unpatched server sits in the corner. The message underneath is serious: fundamentals first. If you want a practical version of that message, our[cybersecurity checklist for CISOs](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/cybersecurity-checklist-for-cisos-2026-resilience-guide) walks through the basics in order.


### Shadow IT and the ticket queue


Shadow IT memes are funny because every security team has found an unapproved tool holding real company data. The ticketing-system memes work the other way: they poke fun at the queue while quietly admitting that it documents issues, prioritizes work, centralizes communication, allocates resources and supports compliance. Both are a reminder that the unglamorous process is often what protects you.


## Why security questionnaires are the funniest pain of all


One topic turns up in security humor again and again, and it belongs to the people who sell software to businesses: the security questionnaire. Anyone in a GRC, sales engineering or compliance role knows the scene. A deal is nearly closed, the buyer's risk team sends a spreadsheet with several hundred questions, and it arrives on a Friday afternoon with a deadline on Monday.


The humor comes from a few predictable places:


- **The same question, asked 40 ways.** "Do you encrypt data at rest?" appears as a yes/no, a paragraph and a dropdown, sometimes within one file.
- **The mystery owner.** Nobody is sure who last answered the question about backup retention, or where that answer lives.
- **The sales and security tug-of-war.** Sales wants it back tomorrow; security wants every answer to be accurate. Both are right.
- **The format roulette.** Spreadsheets, web portals, PDFs and Word files, each with its own quirks.


It is funny because it is relatable, and relatable because it is a process problem. We cover the formats and the mistakes people make in our guide on[how to answer security questionnaires](https://skypher.co/post/how-to-answer-security-questionnaires) , and our piece on[cybersecurity best practices for questionnaires](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/top-cybersecurity-best-practices-2026-questionnaires) shows how to keep answers consistent so the joke stops being your week.


## Can humor actually improve security communication?


Yes, when it has a job to do. Security professionals have been making this case for years, and the evidence is more than anecdotal.


ISC2 describes humor as a way to humanize dry topics and act as a "Trojan horse" for serious information in its piece on[making security awareness training a cultural keystone](https://www.isc2.org/Insights/2026/02/security-awareness-training) . The same article describes one program where phishing jokes and playful scenarios turned training into a conversation starter, and over 95% of staff completed it on time. That is one program, not a guarantee, but it shows what is possible when training stops feeling like punishment.


At the ISC2 Congress, a session on[humor as a communication tool](https://www.isc2.org/Insights/2025/11/isc2congress-humor-as-tool) made two points worth keeping. Humor can help reach audiences, explain complex subjects and make training more memorable. And it should serve a communication goal, not be the message itself.


A large-scale example comes from retail.[Decathlon's 2021 cybersecurity awareness campaign](https://medium.com/decathlondigital/it-takes-only-one-putting-the-spotlight-on-decathlon-technologys-2021-cybersecurity-61279172eb38) used humorous comparisons, including shared public Wi-Fi and a public toothbrush, and launched across 85 countries. The comparisons work because they take an abstract risk and attach it to something instantly gross and instantly understood.


There is also research behind the idea that wording matters. A[study on designing effective security messages](https://jyx.jyu.fi/bitstream/handle/123456789/63605/johnstonwarkentinetalspeaktheirlanguage.pdf;jsessionid=A872B0B12BE6585357EACFA0CC35B03E?sequence=1) (Johnston et al., 2018) suggests that personally relevant language, such as aligning the message with organizational identity, significantly affects how employees think about and respond to security communications. A joke about a situation your own staff recognizes is personally relevant almost by definition.


If you are building or refreshing a program, these pages go further on the training side: our[staff security training program guide](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/staff-security-training-a-2026-program-guide) and our look at[how to choose and run security awareness courses](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/security-awareness-courses) .


## How to use security humor at work without it backfiring


A joke that lands in a team chat can fall flat in an all-hands meeting. These guidelines come from the ISC2 session and the broader practice of professionals who use humor in training.


1. **Pick a goal first.** Decide what you want people to remember: report suspicious email, turn on MFA, update the laptop. Then choose the joke that points at that action.
2. **Make the target the situation, not the person.** Avoid jokes that blame individuals for incidents or single out a colleague. Laughing at "the password everyone picks" is fine; laughing at Dave from accounting is not.
3. **Be inclusive and culturally aware.** What is funny in one office or country may not translate. Decathlon's campaign was translated into at least ten languages and localized for some countries, which is a useful reminder that humor needs adapting.
4. **Mind the timing.** ISC2 guidance advises avoiding jokes about sensitive company events such as layoffs. A breach that is still being investigated is not a punchline either.
5. **Pilot before you scale.** Experts recommend a low-risk pilot to gauge how your audience responds before putting humor into larger presentations or campaigns.
6. **Add a visual.**[Fortra's collection of cybersecurity jokes](https://www.fortra.com/blog/35-cybersecurity-jokes-make-any-security-geek-chuckle-or-groan) notes that this kind of humor tends to work best paired with graphics or visual aids in meetings and presentations.
7. **Never let a joke replace the procedure.** Every funny line about phishing should sit next to the real instruction: where to report it, who to call, which approved resource to open.


That last point matters most. A meme can make people look; only a clear process makes them act. If you are choosing what that process should include, our[security awareness training overview](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/security-awareness-programs-cut-human-risk-35-percent-2026) is a good next read, and fintech teams may prefer our[list of essential trainings for fintech leaders](https://skypher.co/post/security-awareness-trainings-fintech-leaders-en) .


## What our own team finds funniest


It is no accident that so many jokes revolve around repetition. Security teams repeat themselves constantly: the same reminder, the same explanation, the same answer to the same question. The fix for repetition is to capture the right answer once and reuse it. That goes for awareness messages and, as we will get to below, for questionnaires.


Here is a small test you can run with your own team. Collect the five jokes people forward most in your chat channels. Group them by theme using the table above. You will probably find that the themes map to your real friction points. That list is a free, honest roadmap of where process, training or tooling needs attention.

## FAQ


### What is a good cybersecurity joke for a presentation?


Choose one that points at the action you want people to take. For example, "Multifactor authentication is like a seatbelt: everyone agrees it is a great idea until they have to buckle it" leads straight into a slide on enabling MFA. Pair it with a visual and follow it with the real instruction.


### Why are cybersecurity memes so popular with security teams?


They reflect shared frustrations such as unused tools, blame after incidents, understaffed teams and users who resist basic controls. ISACA's analysis argues that this is why they resonate: the humor exposes real organizational contradictions. Sharing them also works as a quick way to cope together.


### Is it appropriate to share cybersecurity memes at work?


Usually, yes, with some care. Keep the humor inclusive, avoid targeting individuals or touching sensitive events like layoffs or an active incident, and try it on a small audience first. Always link the joke to the approved procedure so it never stands in for real security advice.


### Can humor make security awareness training more effective?


It can help. ISC2 reports that humor can make training more engaging and memorable, and describes one program where playful phishing scenarios led to over 95% on-time completion. Humor works best as a way to support a clear goal rather than as the content itself.
